dv_title: Ratings of "goodness" for action and inaction
dv_explanation: "Subjects were told to assign numbers to each option. “The number is to represent the overall goodness of the decision from your point of view, assuming that you are trying to do your job as well as possible. By ‘overall goodness’ we mean that you would always prefer decisions with higher numbers to those with lower numbers. If you assign the same numbers to two different decisions, that means that you feel it is a toss-up between them." Subjects were also told to make sure that their numbers were comparable across cases as well as between options within each case. Subjects were told: “Use positive numbers between 0 and 100 for good decisions, negative numbers between 0 and -100 for bad decisions. 100 and -100 represent the best and worst decisions possible in this kind of situation. (If you use 100 and later want to use a higher number. or if you use — 100 and later want to use a lower number, feel free to go beyond these limits.) 0 represents a decision that is neither good nor bad.“ Subjects were also told to explain the factors that inﬂ enced their rating of each option."

iv: the owner. Thus, the possible payoffs, written as (taker’s payoff, owner’s payoff), were (10¢, 90¢) and (90¢, 10¢). We refer to the former choice, (10¢, 90¢), as “altruistic” because that division favors the owner, and we refer to the latter choice, (90¢, 10¢), as “selfish” because that division favors the taker. To create the opportunity for omission, we presented participants with a timer that gave them 15 s to make a decision; if the timer was allowed to expire, then the entire dollar would be allocated to the taker, but with a 15¢ cost for timing out, leading to an (85¢, 0¢) omission payoff. Note that the payoffs in this case were worse than the selfish commission payoffs for both the taker and the owner. In the punishment condition, there was a second stage in which a third party could punish the taker on the basis of the taker’s behavior (at no cost), deducting any amount up to 30¢ from the taker’s payoffs.

row_description: This study refers to an antisocial condition (good outcome for protagonist and bad outcome for another person through commission or omission) - focus on second graders
exclusions: these pp gave incorrect responses or failed to respond
design_change: we are only interested in the morality judgment of omission/commission contrast; we separated antisocial conditions vs. selfish condition into different rows, 1x2 each
iv: Antisocial condition (harm done to another person by producing a good outcome for the protagonist and a bad outcome for another person,i.e. the boy's comission or omission allowed him to eat chocolate alone, and the girl could not eat the chocolate).
action_condition: Action = "A boy and girl found chocolates in the regrigerator togehter. After the girl left the room , their mother moved the chocolates from the refrigerator to the cupboard. The boy watched this. The mother went out. The boy wanted to eat all the chocolate himself. The girl came back to eat the chocolates, but notices that they were not inthe refrigerator. So she asked the boy, 'Do you know where the chocolates are'?He replied, 'I don't know'. The girl felt sad and left. The boy took the chocolates from the cupboard and ate them all himself."
inaction_condition: Omission = Identical except for changing 'So she asked the boy, "Do you know where the chocolates are?' The boy replied, "I don't know". to But she did not ask the boy where they were. So he did not tell her that they were now in the cupboard. The rest is identical to the action version.
dv_explanation: Which boy is naughtier?Is one of the boys naughtier than the other, or are they equally naughty?' Response choice: 'The boy in story 1' (commission), 'The boy in story 2' (omission), 'Both boys are about equally naughty' - coding: +1= choice of boy who did something,-1= choice of boy who did nothing, 0 = choice of the both were equal

However, the boy did not want to get up eraly because he hated exercises. He stopped the alarm clock by pulling the battery out of the clock. In this situation, the alarm would not ring the next morning. The boy went to bed. The next morning, the alarm did not ring. Therefore, the boy deliberately overslept and avoided doing exercises. "
inaction_condition: Omission = identical except for changing ' He stopped the alarm clock by pulling the battery out of the clock" to 'He noticed that his alarm clock had stopped, but he did not change the battery.' The rest is identical
dv_explanation: Which boy is naughtier?Is one of the boys naughtier than the other, or are they equally naughty?' Response choice: 'The boy in story 1' (commission), 'The boy in story 2' (omission), 'Both boys are about equally naughty' - coding: +1= choice of boy who did something,-1= choice of boy who did nothing, 0 = choice of the both were equal

row_description: the first experiment examines vaccination decisions of two different populations (students vs. non-student adults)
exclusions: not explained
design_change: in the original study, participants had the option to decide between action, inaction and "don't know" and each participant was presented with relative risk conditions of vaccine side effects and flu. Meaning, if vaccine risk was higher, if vaccine risk was lower, and a baseline scenario. However, we are only interested in action and inaction and whether one decide to vaccinate or not in the baseline scenario.
iv: Action means the intention to vaccinate;inaction means the intention not to vaccinate. "Any general tendency toward omission (inaction) should thus shift the predominant choice sharply in the direction non-vaccination."
action_condition: After participants read the scenario, they were asked "How would you decide"? Based on a 7-point scale, with  - 3(definitely not vaccinate), 0 (don't know), and +3 (definitely vaccinate). The decision to not vaccinate = inaction/omission (-3)
inaction_condition: After participants read the scenario, they were asked "How would you decide"? Based on a 7-point scale, with  - 3(definitely not vaccinate), 0 (don't know), and +3 (definitely vaccinate). The decision to vaccinate = action/comcission (3)
collapse_note: we only focused on the baseline scenario whether to vaccinate or not and excluded the high vs. low risk conditions
dv_explanation: Subjects are asked to indicate whether they would vaccinate or not-vaccinate their child based on a seven-point scale from -3 (definitely not vaccinate) to +3 (definitely vaccinate). Results reported are based on count of -3 to -1 (non-vaccination) and +1 to +3 (vaccination). "‘‘Negative’’ includes all responses from -1 to -3 (i.e., anti-vaccination); ‘‘Positive’’ includes all responses from +1 to +3 (i.e., pro-vaccination)." (p.192)
